newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro slams food summit aims as shamefully modest.
newsitem.headline: Castro slams food summit aims as shamefully modest.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro, describing hunger as daily genocide, told a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit on Saturday that the Cold War was over but capitalism and consumerism were killing millions.
"Capitalism, neoliberalism, the laws of a wild market, the external debt, underdevelopment (are) killing so many people in the world," the communist leader said in his address.

The bearded revolutionary and veteran Cold War scourge of capitalism swept into the summit surrounded by tight security after arriving in Rome during the night, and proceeded to denounce its aims as a shameful fig-leaf.
The summit declaration calls on world leaders to work towards halving the number of hungry people in the world from a current 840 million within 20 years.
Asking what "cosmetic solutions" were going to be provided, Castro, who meets Pope John Paul at the Vatican on Tuesday, said: "The very modesty of these goals is shameful."

"If the world is rightly moved by accidents and natural or social catastrophes that bring death to hundreds or thousands of people, why is it not equally moved by that genocide which is taking place every day in front of our eyes?"
The penultimate day of the gathering gave the developing nations the floor after the wealthier countries had made their views known on Friday, and they demanded action.

While the "haves" raised human rights, democracy and corruption as important issues in the fight against hunger and urged poorer countries not to rely on aid alone, the "have nots" spoke of the grinding daily realities of hardship.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said poverty could not be understood without knowing what hunger meant.
Governments claimed they were aware of issues concerning hunger and poverty (but) "political will that is so essential to tackle hunger seems to be lacking," he said.
Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, one of the few speakers from developed nations in the morning session, said the developed countries carried a particular responsibility.
"We cannot ignore an estimated billion people living in abject poverty," he said. "International solidarity is crucial."
Castro blasted military spending and arms sales to developing states, asking "why are increasingly sophisticated weapons still being produced after the Cold War is over?"

Sheikh Hasina, prime minister of Bangladesh, whose country was at the centre of a crisis at the last food summit in 1974, also targeted lingering Cold War attitudes, saying "the threat of conflict between East and West is well behind us".

And she said the hungry were asking one question: "What are we all and the world powers waiting for to use the huge resources swallowed up by our budgets for human destruction to engage in outright battle with poverty and hunger?"
The Food Summit has been dominated by debate about the crisis in Central Africa, where hundreds of thousands of starving have begun trekking back to Rwanda.
Delegates have called repeatedly for action to prevent such scenes happening again and to avert widespread unrest in countries in the Great Lakes region.
Angolan President Jose Eduardo Dos Santos said his country supported a multinational force for the region and was concerned about instability on its northern border with Zaire.
The problems were highlighted when soldiers in the Central African Republic were reported to have launched a mutiny after forcibly taking weapons from an armoury.

The country's president, Ange-Felix Patasse, denied that a mutiny was under way and said common criminals who had escaped were trying to spread panic. "Nothing abnormal," was his response when asked by Reuters at the summit.
